tweets.text: Today we announced the Claude-led discovery of a molecular machine that we suspect could represent a new gene editing mechanism. Its precise function, biotechnological utility (if any), or level of significance is not yet clear, but at minimum it is work I would have been proud to do as a PhD student. The work was done mostly, though not entirely, by Claude: our life sciences team suggested a broad area of research, Claude read through the literature and a bunch of genome data and discovered something interesting, then Claude proposed experiments to verify the discovery and our team carried them out. It’s easy to dismiss this as a one-off or curiosity, but we’ve repeatedly seen a pattern where AI performance in new intellectual domains goes from weak to superhuman in a matter of a few years. In 2023 models struggled to do math at the level of an average high-school student. In 2024 they started to do well on math competitions for the best high-schoolers in the country, in 2025 they started to solve minor open problems, in early 2026 more significant open problems, and in late 2026 they are beginning to solve the top few open problems in all of mathematics. We believe AI for biology is on a similar exponential trend. The main difference between biology and mathematics, of course, is that math can be done purely theoretically, while biology requires experimentation. Some have used this to draw the conclusion that AI’s utility in biology will be limited. We think this is wrong. As we’ve demonstrated today, humans can collaborate with AI to perform the experiments, validate key results in a few weeks and, if necessary, work with the AI to iterate on what they find. Eventually it may even be possible for Claude itself to safely perform the experiments by autonomously controlling lab equipment, with appropriate safeguards in place, but we aren’t doing that today (our lab is also a BSL1/BSL2 facility that doesn't handle materials dangerous to humans). More broadly, biomedical advancement has many stages — from fundamental biology discoveries, to translational research, to drug discovery, clinical trials, and finally the actual delivery of medicines and health care to patients. We are also interested in these later stages, but even simply accelerating the first stage of fundamental biological discoveries has the potential to speed up and broaden the entire pipeline. Improving our understanding of biology and sharpening biologists’ tools can drive forward all of the later stages, for example by identifying new drug targets, finding new therapeutic modalities, allowing for more precise measurement, and speeding up the experimental loop which itself further accelerates our understanding of biology. This will not in itself speed up clinical trial times, but if it succeeds it could greatly increase the number of promising candidates that go into the pipeline — an increase in throughput even though latency remains. In Machines of Loving Grace, I wrote about AI’s potential to “cure most diseases in 5-10 years” — a goal that sounds impossible, but one I believe is just barely possible if AI is applied to every stage of the pipeline. The first step is showing that AI can first help with, and then drive, biological discoveries. Claude’s discovery is the latest in a line of related prior work that goes back decades, beginning with systems like CRISPR, and continuing with discoveries like the bridge recombinase and VIPR in the past few years. Recently, there has been heightened interest in systems based on reverse transcriptase (RT) enzymes, the enzyme underlying the system Claude identified. And most recently, a Stanford team working independently described a novel RT system with an associated non-coding array that is in some ways similar to the one Claude found, though they are distinct systems that evolved independently from each other. I believe that we’re at the very beginning of finding such systems and developing them into powerful tools for biotechnology. I’m proud of the resources Anthropic has invested in accelerating the public benefits of AI through the life sciences, and we’re aiming both to grow our life sciences team and to work with other scientists to extend this approach to a broad range of problems. If you have a proposal for a research collaboration or are interested in joining our life sciences team, please reach out. Anthropic (@AnthropicAI) Claude has discovered a previously unknown enzyme system hidden in the DNA of bacteriophages. Beside the enzyme’s gene sits a long array of repeating DNA—a structure that looks somewhat similar to CRISPR. We don’t yet understand what this system does, but only a handful of known systems share its features, and all of them are able to cut, copy, and paste DNA. Historically, the discovery of such programmable systems has helped revolutionize medicine. CRISPR, for instance, is now the foundation of genetic medicines. But it will take much more work to learn what this system does, and whether it can be put to similar use. 2/2 Second, on the messaging around AI. I do not agree that my messaging has been disproportionately negative. In fact it has been about equally balanced between risks and benefits: I’ve written one major essay about each, and even in interviews where I discuss the risks, I make sure to frequently mention the incredible benefits as well as proposing possible solutions to the risks (short clips from my interviews that end up on social media tend to be disproportionately negative, as that gets clicks). In fact, I wrote Machines of Loving Grace because I didn’t feel the AI industry was painting an inspiring enough picture of how the technology could radically transform the world for the better. The bulk of the essay is devoted to refuting skepticism of AI’s potential in health and biology, and showing why I think it will actually be possible to cure most human disease in ~5-10 years, as crazy as it may sound to ordinary people and frankly to biologists as well (I used to be one!). And, if you read my most recent essay (Policy on the AI Exponential), I discuss concrete proposals for how to streamline the FDA process to make sure the deluge of AI-accelerated drugs isn’t slowed down by the regulatory process. I feel the urgency here: I lost my father to Hepatitis C only a few years before the development of direct-acting antivirals (sofosbuvir), which cure 95% of patients and probably would have cured him. I do agree that the public has a negative view of AI (and that this is a big problem), but I don’t think it is primarily caused by me or any other AI leader warning about AI’s risks. I think it is fundamentally a crisis of trust. I think that ordinary people don’t trust companies, governments, or the tech industry and always suspect that we are cooking up some new way to screw them over. The causes of this go back decades and AI is just the latest iteration of it. I don’t think that a glitzy marketing campaign with a positive spin (which some have advocated that Anthropic do) is the way to win back that trust — at this point, saying that AI will cure cancer is more a cliche than it is inspiring, and most people think it is deceptive. The thing that will work is *actually curing cancer*. I think by far the most accurate criticism of AI companies including Anthropic is that we haven’t yet delivered on our big promises to benefit the world. That is totally on us, and I think it’s the criticism you should be making, instead of all this stuff about messaging and marketing. We are however doing our best to fix this: Anthropic is ramping up its efforts very quickly in biology and medicine, and we hope to have incredible results in the coming years and some early glimmers in the coming months. When we’ve actually accomplished something real, the whole world will hear about it, as loudly as possible, you have my word on that. But until then I don’t want to make empty promises, and in the meantime I feel compelled to speak honestly about the very real risks of AI and how to address them. Honesty is the right thing on the merits, and in terms of public credibility and trust it is no worse than, and may in fact be better than, an approach that ignores or distracts from risks which people instinctively understand are real.

1/2 Thanks Gavin for an especially thoughtful exchange. I don't usually spend much time on social media but I wanted to engage here because it really brings out the heart of an important conversation. First, on regulation, I think that “either concentrate it in the hands of a chosen few companies and politicians via regulation or distribute it widely” is a false choice. I know that there’s a sort of Silicon Valley shorthand where regulation = regulatory capture = concentration of power, but I’ve always found this to be an overly simplified picture of the world. Many people outside this bubble think of regulation as something that constrains corporate power and benefits ordinary people. I don’t necessarily agree with that perspective either, rather I think it’s complicated and really depends on what the “regulation” consists of. But in particular I think that those in the “regulation = regulatory capture = concentration of power” frame often underrate the decentralizing power of objective and fair institutional processes. A crude analogy is that the formal court system can sometimes feel stuffy and elitist, but it does a much better job of defending the rights of vulnerable individuals than the alternative, mob justice. At their best, institutions can vest power in ideas rather than people, and thereby decentralize that power. This is why Anthropic has always made its policy proposals very carefully. We try very hard to make proposals that disadvantage (slow down) frontier AI companies while *advantaging* smaller competitors. California’s SB53 (which we supported), and even the much-maligned SB 1047 (which we were ambivalent on), completely exempt any company below a certain amount of revenue or model training costs from being covered at all (it was $500M for SB 53, lower for 1047 but we objected to that). More recently the testing process we’ve advocated for at CAISI and the White House involves more rigorous tests for frontier models than off-frontier models — something that differentially advantages challengers. Similarly, the “Pacing the Frontier” letter envisions (or at least Anthropic’s preferred implementation of it envisions) modulating the pace of the very best models while not constraining those who are catching up. This hurts the business interests of the frontier labs and helps challengers, including open-weights! Overall my view is that AI is *structurally* a technology that tends to concentrate power, for reasons that have nothing to do with regulation (more to do with the extreme implications of the scaling laws). Open-weights do help some with this but are nowhere near a sufficient solution because they simply shift the concentration somewhat to those with the most compute and chips (which are roughly the frontier labs plus maybe hardware providers). By contrast I think the right “rules of the road” can simultaneously (a) address AI’s cyber/bio/alignment risks, (b) institutionally constrain the power of the frontier AI companies, and (c) leave room for open-weights models while also addressing the specific risks that they bring. BTW I do not think that the events of the last few months have “failed to result in [my] preferred regulatory path”. The approach that the Trump administration is reported to be taking — pre-deployment testing for frontier models, and also testing of open-weights models when they get closer to the frontier — is one that I am very supportive of, though of course I have to see the details to be sure. I am also supportive of Demis Hassabis’ ideas around a FINRA-like entity. This contrasts with six months ago when most of the industry was still pushing for preemption of all state regulation and no apparent federal approach either. Gavin Baker (@GavinSBaker) Sholto, thank you for setting the record straight. Larger issue is that multiple very serious people in Silicon Valley have heard some variation of this and believe it to be true. And the reason it is believable to so many is that it is consistent with Dario’s public messaging and what he outlined in the essay you shared: this technology *might* be dangerous for humans in multiple ways, could lead to extreme concentration of economic power (as outlined in the essay) and therefore needs to be regulated thoughtfully. I agree with the potential risks and I believe Dario makes all of these arguments in good faith. As discussed on the pod, if one agrees that AI *might* be dangerous, there are two ways to address this potential risk. Either concentrate it in the hands of a chosen few companies and politicians via regulation or distribute it widely. Essentially boils down to whether one believes AI is too dangerous to concentrate or too dangerous to distribute. There are reasonable arguments on both sides, but I profoundly agree with Zuckerberg’s statement that: “The notion that AI is so dangerous that the only safe path is an extreme concentration of power seems inherently problematic. Historically, hoping that an absolute power will benevolently provide for humanity if sufficiently enlightened has not led to safe or positive outcomes.” And as Dario says in the aforementioned essay, “some may object that we can simply keep AIs in check with a balance of power between many AI systems, as we do with humans.” I believe this is the best path forward: I want as many AIs as possible to maximize the odds that one shares my own particular values. And as Dario notes, no human has ever been able to take over the world. At this point, I think safe to say that Dario has lost the argument. His messaging has failed to result in his preferred regulatory path. The fact that the only solution to the recent incident where an unreleased advanced OpenAI model hacked Hugging Face was an open-source model likely ended any chance of strict near-term regulation. Essentially every major company other than Anthropic has signed Jensen’s letter. However, Dario’s messaging has been massively helpful to efforts to ban datacenters here in America. I suspect we will see anti-datacenter advocacy groups runnings ads using clips of Dario warning about how dangerous AI could be for humans. His good faith efforts in favor of regulation are now increasing the odds that AI will not be beneficial for Americans and humans everywhere. I believe that there is a reasonable chance AI might help us cure most forms of disease such that we have extended lifespans and can enjoy these long lives in an abundant Star Trek like future. That is the future that I want and I think Dario is decreasing the odds of that future at this point. He is about to be the CEO of one of the most important public companies in the world and given that the pro-regulatory effort has failed (at least for now), I respectfully think he should make an effort to be a more positive advocate for his own industry. And if I am wrong and we do need to regulate this technology, he will be a more effective advocate for this in the future having been open-minded to the alternative. And for the sake of clarity and as I outlined on the pod, I think Anthropic has deep competitive advantages and is an amazing company. Ironically, the main risk I saw to Anthropic a few months ago was nationalization as a result of Dario’s own rhetoric and behavior. — https://nitter.kareem.one/GavinSBaker/status/2088611616577253502#m

6 days and $40,000 of compute with GPT-5.6 Sol to find a critical vulnerability in Chrome, claiming Google’s first full-chain reward in 2026 for a vulnerability that would affect an estimated 1 billion users. Highlights the opportunity for defenders to utilize these tools to secure their software to unprecedented levels: Oege de Moor (@oegerikus) For the second time in Google Chrome’s history, Google awarded a $250,000 bounty for a full-chain exploit… to @XBOW . Here’s the full story: At an all-hands at the start of 2026 in Malta, I set the team a crazy challenge. A full-chain exploit of Chrome by the annual Black Hat cybersecurity conference in August. I believed there were few better tests of whether @XBOW could move beyond web applications to desktop software, servers and devices. Chrome is one of the most hardened pieces of software on the planet, used by more than half the world’s population. A full-chain exploit lets an attacker take total control of a machine, where they can read every email, password and bank login the user types. You don’t need to download anything or click a phishing link. Visiting the wrong site is enough. So @moyix , Andres Luksenberg, Baul Lee, and Willem Pinckaers took on the challenge along with a fifth teammate: OpenAI's GPT-5.6 Sol. They built a chain they thought would win, but Google told us they already knew one of the bugs. We were already in Las Vegas for Black Hat and DEF CON, and the team didn’t want to go home without the win. So Brendan and the agents built a new exploit in just 6 days. We submitted it to Google and waited. The news came through that we'd done what should’ve been impossible. A full-chain bounty of $250,000, the first awarded under Google’s 2026 rules. It took just 6 days and $40,000 of compute to construct an exploit that affects a billion users of Chrome on Windows. An intelligence-agency veteran told me his team used to spend 6 months on this kind of vulnerability. My takeaway: the cost of finding truly critical vulnerabilities is collapsing, for attackers and defenders alike. Restricting powerful models is not the answer; GPT-5.6 Sol is already public. But defenders have one advantage attackers never will: they can test their own code first. Assume your software is exploitable. Whoever is hunting your bugs has the same building blocks we did. This is cause for urgency but not panic. XBOW is now developing an autonomous product for testing compiled software (desktop applications, servers, embedded devices), and partnering with the world’s top organizations to design that product. If you’d like to be one of them, get in touch. P.S. Restart Chrome whenever the Update button appears! — http://nitter.meowing.monster/oegerikus/status/2110032518674018367#m

People seem confused about why Tesla is getting so much backlash over its new "flying Roadster." For those of us who were once genuinely enthusiastic about Tesla, this isn't about hating innovation. It's about a long history of broken promises, misleading expectations, and increasingly absurd marketing. Tesla unveiled the second-generation Roadster in 2017, took customer deposits, and promised deliveries in 2020. Six years past that deadline, it still hasn't delivered the car. Instead, it's demonstrating an even more outrageous version with features that will likely never make it into production. The original 2nd gen Roadster would still be an amazing car today. Why not just deliver what was promised? Then there's Full Self-Driving. Tesla marketed the idea that Model 3 owners could turn their cars into income-generating robotaxis. That never materialized. Even if the technology eventually gets there, the opportunity has already passed for many early buyers. Timing matters. Delivering something a decade late isn't fulfilling the promise you sold to customers. And then there's Solar Roof. Unveiled in 2016 as a revolutionary approach to residential solar, it struggled with costs, installation challenges, and adoption far below expectations. After nearly a decade, Tesla discontinued it entirely in August 2026. Another grand vision abandoned, leaving existing customers with a discontinued product to maintain. Then came the Cybertruck, marketed as a nearly indestructible, revolutionary truck. Instead, we got a vehicle with questionable build quality, numerous recalls, expensive repairs, disappointing results in several real-world off-road tests, and specifications that fell short of the original promises. It literally looks like a dumpster, but aesthetics aside, the collapsing demand speaks volumes about the reality of what Tesla delivered. Another heavily hyped product that fell dramatically short of expectations. This is how consumer trust erodes. Not through one disappointment, but through years of accumulating them. And this is part of the reason why many people who were once enthusiastic about Tesla have become critical and cynical about it. But there's something even more fundamental here: Tesla has completely departed from the grounded, practical vision that made so many of us enthusiastic about the company in the first place. Electric cars were ambitious, but the idea was grounded in reality. People could charge at home, infrastructure could gradually expand, technology could improve, and millions of ordinary people could eventually benefit. There was a realistic path toward mass adoption. What the hell does a flying Roadster powered by compressed-air thrusters have to do with any of that? It's an expensive, impractical engineering stunt with enormous packaging, safety, and regulatory challenges, and no credible near-term path toward mass-market usefulness. Modern electric cars already achieve ridiculous acceleration without this nonsense. What practical problem does it solve? Who actually needs it? When will ordinary consumers benefit? And watching Tesla fans compare this experimental prototype in a Roadster-shaped shell to actual production vehicles people can buy today is ridiculous. What's especially infuriating is the cult-like mentality surrounding all of this. You can't point out the history of failed promises, question the practicality, or demand realistic timelines without being accused of being a "hater" or having "Elon derangement syndrome." Tesla deserves recognition for helping make electric cars a reality, but that success doesn't give it a blank check to keep marketing increasingly fantastical promises while failing to deliver on previous commitments. This isn't hatred. It's disappointment from people who once believed in the company, watched it accomplish extraordinary things, and have since watched it increasingly substitute practical innovation with spectacle and promises. Elon fanboys are also ignoring a bigger pattern that goes beyond Tesla. What made many of us enthusiastic about Elon and Tesla and in the first place was a grounded vision of technological progress that could genuinely improve millions of lives. Electric cars were ambitious, but practical, achievable, and useful to ordinary people. Now we're supposed to get excited about flying cars with compressed-air thrusters that have no credible path to mass adoption and solve no meaningful problem for the average consumer. It's the same kind of thinking behind marketing the colonization of Mars as some urgent necessity for humanity's survival. There's nothing wrong with space exploration, but Earth isn't about to become uninhabitable because of the Sun. We're talking about geological timescales, while humanity faces enormous problems RIGHT NOW: poverty, hunger, access to education, corruption, abuse of power, wars, and a lack of government accountability. We have plenty of very real problems to solve before worrying about humanity's survival on another planet. And then there's DOGE. I was genuinely excited about the original idea of making government more efficient, reducing waste, and increasing accountability. Instead, we got questionable savings figures, inexperienced people making sweeping decisions, serious concerns over access to sensitive personal information, and an initiative that ultimately fizzled out without delivering its grand promises. Another enormous narrative that fell apart when confronted with reality. That's what makes all of this so frustrating. It's not that we stopped believing in technological progress. It's that we've watched someone who once pursued grounded, transformative ideas increasingly embrace fantastical promises, political spectacle, and questionable narratives disconnected from practical reality. And somehow, pointing out this history of disappointment gets you labeled a "hater" or accused of having "Elon derangement syndrome." The problem isn't dreaming big. It's repeatedly selling people those dreams, failing to deliver, and then expecting everyone to applaud the next, even more ridiculous promise without asking what happened to the last one. The world doesn't need more spectacular promises. It needs practical solutions to real problems, honest expectations, and accountability for what was promised. That's what made Tesla exciting in the first place, and that's what so many of us feel has been betrayed.

Earlier and more accurate forecasting can help protect communities by giving them more time to prepare, and we are grateful that Google’s WeatherNext model was able to assist the @NWSNHC 's expert forecasters. Based on initial evaluations, here's how our model supported the response to #Isaias : - Tracking the Hurricane’s Path: WeatherNext was the most accurate model on the storm’s track. While traditional physics models predicted landfall closer to New Orleans, WeatherNext correctly predicted a path further east. This allowed NHC forecasters to highlight the potential for wind and storm surge impacts in the Florida Panhandle from their very first forecast. - More Time to Prepare: Up to three days before landfall, our model consistently predicted its eventual location in the Florida Panhandle to within 60 km or less, supporting the NHC as they honed in on a track toward the Florida Panhandle and issued hurricane watches and warnings to give officials in Florida, Alabama, and Mississippi more time to prepare. - Early Indications about Intensity: Early on, WeatherNext accurately predicted the intensification to a major hurricane. Alongside the regional hurricane models HWRF and HMON, WeatherNext’s intensity forecasts helped NHC forecasters to predict that the Isaias would approach the coast as a category 2 hurricane from the very first advisory. Giving communities more time and more accurate warnings is critical for protecting lives and livelihoods. While model performance varies from storm to storm, Isaias reflects our broader findings. In our recent @Nature paper co-authored with NHC forecasters, evaluating 200+ global tropical cyclones, we found our model provides ~1 day of additional lead time for both track and intensity. It’s been an honor for the @GoogleDeepMind and @GoogleResearch teams to work alongside NHC forecasters. By combining AI, physics models, satellite data, and the crucial expertise of meteorologists, we're excited to keep pushing the boundaries of forecasting to help protect communities.

Il s'agit de la capacité de modifier précisément le code génétique d'un organisme (l'ADN) pour corriger des défauts ou introduire de nouvelles propriétés.
Désigne une intelligence artificielle très avancée, repoussant les limites de ce qui est techniquement réalisable à un moment donné.

Un programme d'intelligence artificielle capable de prendre des décisions, d'interagir avec son environnement et d'accomplir des tâches de manière autonome, parfois en collaborant avec d'autres agents.

Ce terme désigne l'effort de s'assurer que les systèmes d'IA se comportent de manière cohérente avec les intentions humaines et les valeurs sociétales, sans dévier vers des objectifs imprévus ou dangereux.
C'est une méthode d'entraînement spécialisée qui permet d'adapter un grand modèle d'IA pré-existant à une tâche très spécifique avec beaucoup moins de données et de puissance de calcul.

highlights.text_fr: Aujourd'hui, nous avons annoncé la découverte, menée par Claude, d'une machine moléculaire qui, nous le soupçonnons, pourrait représenter un nouveau mécanisme d'édition génique. Sa fonction précise, son utilité biotechnologique (le cas échéant) ou son niveau de signification ne sont pas encore clairs, mais à minima, c'est un travail dont j'aurais été fier de faire en tant qu'étudiant en doctorat. Le travail a été réalisé principalement, bien que pas entièrement, par Claude : notre équipe des sciences de la vie a suggéré un vaste domaine de recherche, Claude a parcouru la littérature et une quantité de données génomiques et a découvert quelque chose d'intéressant, puis Claude a proposé des expériences pour vérifier la découverte et notre équipe les a réalisées. Il est facile de rejeter cela comme un coup de chance ou une curiosité, mais nous avons observé à plusieurs reprises un modèle où la performance de l'IA dans de nouveaux domaines intellectuels passe de faible à surhumaine en quelques années. En 2023, les modèles avaient du mal à faire des mathématiques au niveau d'un lycéen moyen. En 2024, ils ont commencé à bien réussir les concours de mathématiques pour les meilleurs lycéens du pays, en 2025 ils ont commencé à résoudre des problèmes ouverts mineurs, début 2026 des problèmes ouverts plus significatifs, et fin 2026 ils commencent à résoudre les quelques problèmes ouverts majeurs de toutes les mathématiques. Nous pensons que l'IA pour la biologie suit une tendance exponentielle similaire. La principale différence entre la biologie et les mathématiques, bien sûr, est que les mathématiques peuvent être faites purement théoriquement, tandis que la biologie nécessite de l'expérimentation. Certains ont utilisé cela pour en conclure que l'utilité de l'IA en biologie sera limitée. Nous pensons que c'est faux. Comme nous l'avons démontré aujourd'hui, les humains peuvent collaborer avec l'IA pour réaliser les expériences, valider les résultats clés en quelques semaines et, si nécessaire, travailler avec l'IA pour itérer sur ce qu'ils trouvent. Il pourrait même être possible à terme pour Claude lui-même de réaliser les expériences en toute sécurité en contrôlant de manière autonome l'équipement de laboratoire, avec des mesures de protection appropriées, mais nous ne faisons pas cela aujourd'hui (notre laboratoire est également une installation BSL1/BSL2 qui ne manipule pas de matériaux dangereux pour les humains). Plus largement, le progrès biomédical comporte de nombreuses étapes — des découvertes fondamentales en biologie à la recherche translationnelle, en passant par la découverte de médicaments, les essais cliniques et enfin la livraison effective des médicaments et des soins de santé aux patients. Nous nous intéressons également à ces étapes ultérieures, mais même le simple fait d'accélérer la première étape des découvertes biologiques fondamentales a le potentiel d'accélérer et d'élargir l'ensemble du processus. Améliorer notre compréhension de la biologie et affiner les outils des biologistes peut faire avancer toutes les étapes ultérieures, par exemple en identifiant de nouvelles cibles médicamenteuses, en trouvant de nouvelles modalités thérapeutiques, en permettant des mesures plus précises et en accélérant la boucle expérimentale qui, elle-même, accélère notre compréhension de la biologie. Cela n'accélérera pas en soi les délais des essais cliniques, mais si cela réussit, cela pourrait augmenter considérablement le nombre de candidats prometteurs qui entrent dans le processus — une augmentation du débit même si la latence demeure. Dans Machines of Loving Grace, j'ai écrit sur le potentiel de l'IA à "guérir la plupart des maladies en 5 à 10 ans" — un objectif qui semble impossible, mais que je crois à peine possible si l'IA est appliquée à chaque étape du processus. La première étape est de montrer que l'IA peut d'abord aider, puis mener, les découvertes biologiques. La découverte de Claude est la dernière d'une série de travaux antérieurs similaires qui remontent à des décennies, commençant par des systèmes comme CRISPR, et se poursuivant avec des découvertes comme la recombinase pont et VIPR ces dernières années. Récemment, l'intérêt s'est accru pour les systèmes basés sur les enzymes transcriptase inverse (RT), l'enzyme sous-jacente au système identifié par Claude. Et plus récemment, une équipe de Stanford travaillant indépendamment a décrit un nouveau système RT avec un ensemble non codant associé qui est en quelque sorte similaire à celui trouvé par Claude, bien qu'il s'agisse de systèmes distincts qui ont évolué indépendamment l'un de l'autre. Je crois que nous ne faisons que commencer à trouver de tels systèmes et à les développer en outils puissants pour la biotechnologie. Je suis fier des ressources qu'Anthropic a investies pour accélérer les bénéfices publics de l'IA à travers les sciences de la vie, et nous visons à la fois à développer notre équipe des sciences de la vie et à travailler avec d'autres scientifiques pour étendre cette approche à un large éventail de problèmes. Si vous avez une proposition de collaboration de recherche ou si vous êtes intéressé à rejoindre notre équipe des sciences de la vie, n'hésitez pas à nous contacter. Anthropic (@AnthropicAI) Claude a découvert un système enzymatique jusqu'alors inconnu, caché dans l'ADN des bactériophages. À côté du gène de l'enzyme se trouve une longue séquence d'ADN répétitif — une structure qui ressemble un peu au CRISPR. Nous ne comprenons pas encore ce que fait ce système, mais seule une poignée de systèmes connus partagent ses caractéristiques, et tous sont capables de couper, copier et coller de l'ADN. Historiquement, la découverte de tels systèmes programmables a contribué à révolutionner la médecine. CRISPR, par exemple, est maintenant le fondement des médicaments génétiques. Mais il faudra beaucoup plus de travail pour apprendre ce que fait ce système, et si on peut l'utiliser de manière similaire. highlights.text_original: Today we announced the Claude-led discovery of a molecular machine that we suspect could represent a new gene editing mechanism. Its precise function, biotechnological utility (if any), or level of significance is not yet clear, but at minimum it is work I would have been proud to do as a PhD student. The work was done mostly, though not entirely, by Claude: our life sciences team suggested a broad area of research, Claude read through the literature and a bunch of genome data and discovered something interesting, then Claude proposed experiments to verify the discovery and our team carried them out. It’s easy to dismiss this as a one-off or curiosity, but we’ve repeatedly seen a pattern where AI performance in new intellectual domains goes from weak to superhuman in a matter of a few years. In 2023 models struggled to do math at the level of an average high-school student. In 2024 they started to do well on math competitions for the best high-schoolers in the country, in 2025 they started to solve minor open problems, in early 2026 more significant open problems, and in late 2026 they are beginning to solve the top few open problems in all of mathematics. We believe AI for biology is on a similar exponential trend. The main difference between biology and mathematics, of course, is that math can be done purely theoretically, while biology requires experimentation. Some have used this to draw the conclusion that AI’s utility in biology will be limited. We think this is wrong. As we’ve demonstrated today, humans can collaborate with AI to perform the experiments, validate key results in a few weeks and, if necessary, work with the AI to iterate on what they find. Eventually it may even be possible for Claude itself to safely perform the experiments by autonomously controlling lab equipment, with appropriate safeguards in place, but we aren’t doing that today (our lab is also a BSL1/BSL2 facility that doesn't handle materials dangerous to humans). More broadly, biomedical advancement has many stages — from fundamental biology discoveries, to translational research, to drug discovery, clinical trials, and finally the actual delivery of medicines and health care to patients. We are also interested in these later stages, but even simply accelerating the first stage of fundamental biological discoveries has the potential to speed up and broaden the entire pipeline. Improving our understanding of biology and sharpening biologists’ tools can drive forward all of the later stages, for example by identifying new drug targets, finding new therapeutic modalities, allowing for more precise measurement, and speeding up the experimental loop which itself further accelerates our understanding of biology. This will not in itself speed up clinical trial times, but if it succeeds it could greatly increase the number of promising candidates that go into the pipeline — an increase in throughput even though latency remains. In Machines of Loving Grace, I wrote about AI’s potential to “cure most diseases in 5-10 years” — a goal that sounds impossible, but one I believe is just barely possible if AI is applied to every stage of the pipeline. The first step is showing that AI can first help with, and then drive, biological discoveries. Claude’s discovery is the latest in a line of related prior work that goes back decades, beginning with systems like CRISPR, and continuing with discoveries like the bridge recombinase and VIPR in the past few years. Recently, there has been heightened interest in systems based on reverse transcriptase (RT) enzymes, the enzyme underlying the system Claude identified. And most recently, a Stanford team working independently described a novel RT system with an associated non-coding array that is in some ways similar to the one Claude found, though they are distinct systems that evolved independently from each other. I believe that we’re at the very beginning of finding such systems and developing them into powerful tools for biotechnology. I’m proud of the resources Anthropic has invested in accelerating the public benefits of AI through the life sciences, and we’re aiming both to grow our life sciences team and to work with other scientists to extend this approach to a broad range of problems. If you have a proposal for a research collaboration or are interested in joining our life sciences team, please reach out. Anthropic (@AnthropicAI) Claude has discovered a previously unknown enzyme system hidden in the DNA of bacteriophages. Beside the enzyme’s gene sits a long array of repeating DNA—a structure that looks somewhat similar to CRISPR. We don’t yet understand what this system does, but only a handful of known systems share its features, and all of them are able to cut, copy, and paste DNA. Historically, the discovery of such programmable systems has helped revolutionize medicine. CRISPR, for instance, is now the foundation of genetic medicines. But it will take much more work to learn what this system does, and whether it can be put to similar use. actu.text_fr: Aujourd'hui, nous avons annoncé la découverte, menée par Claude, d'une machine moléculaire qui, nous le soupçonnons, pourrait représenter un nouveau mécanisme d'édition génique. Sa fonction précise, son utilité biotechnologique (le cas échéant) ou son niveau de signification ne sont pas encore clairs, mais à minima, c'est un travail dont j'aurais été fier de faire en tant qu'étudiant en doctorat. Le travail a été réalisé principalement, bien que pas entièrement, par Claude : notre équipe des sciences de la vie a suggéré un vaste domaine de recherche, Claude a parcouru la littérature et une quantité de données génomiques et a découvert quelque chose d'intéressant, puis Claude a proposé des expériences pour vérifier la découverte et notre équipe les a réalisées. Il est facile de rejeter cela comme un coup de chance ou une curiosité, mais nous avons observé à plusieurs reprises un modèle où la performance de l'IA dans de nouveaux domaines intellectuels passe de faible à surhumaine en quelques années. En 2023, les modèles avaient du mal à faire des mathématiques au niveau d'un lycéen moyen. En 2024, ils ont commencé à bien réussir les concours de mathématiques pour les meilleurs lycéens du pays, en 2025 ils ont commencé à résoudre des problèmes ouverts mineurs, début 2026 des problèmes ouverts plus significatifs, et fin 2026 ils commencent à résoudre les quelques problèmes ouverts majeurs de toutes les mathématiques. Nous pensons que l'IA pour la biologie suit une tendance exponentielle similaire. La principale différence entre la biologie et les mathématiques, bien sûr, est que les mathématiques peuvent être faites purement théoriquement, tandis que la biologie nécessite de l'expérimentation. Certains ont utilisé cela pour en conclure que l'utilité de l'IA en biologie sera limitée. Nous pensons que c'est faux. Comme nous l'avons démontré aujourd'hui, les humains peuvent collaborer avec l'IA pour réaliser les expériences, valider les résultats clés en quelques semaines et, si nécessaire, travailler avec l'IA pour itérer sur ce qu'ils trouvent. Il pourrait même être possible à terme pour Claude lui-même de réaliser les expériences en toute sécurité en contrôlant de manière autonome l'équipement de laboratoire, avec des mesures de protection appropriées, mais nous ne faisons pas cela aujourd'hui (notre laboratoire est également une installation BSL1/BSL2 qui ne manipule pas de matériaux dangereux pour les humains). Plus largement, le progrès biomédical comporte de nombreuses étapes — des découvertes fondamentales en biologie à la recherche translationnelle, en passant par la découverte de médicaments, les essais cliniques et enfin la livraison effective des médicaments et des soins de santé aux patients. Nous nous intéressons également à ces étapes ultérieures, mais même le simple fait d'accélérer la première étape des découvertes biologiques fondamentales a le potentiel d'accélérer et d'élargir l'ensemble du processus. Améliorer notre compréhension de la biologie et affiner les outils des biologistes peut faire avancer toutes les étapes ultérieures, par exemple en identifiant de nouvelles cibles médicamenteuses, en trouvant de nouvelles modalités thérapeutiques, en permettant des mesures plus précises et en accélérant la boucle expérimentale qui, elle-même, accélère notre compréhension de la biologie. Cela n'accélérera pas en soi les délais des essais cliniques, mais si cela réussit, cela pourrait augmenter considérablement le nombre de candidats prometteurs qui entrent dans le processus — une augmentation du débit même si la latence demeure. Dans Machines of Loving Grace, j'ai écrit sur le potentiel de l'IA à "guérir la plupart des maladies en 5 à 10 ans" — un objectif qui semble impossible, mais que je crois à peine possible si l'IA est appliquée à chaque étape du processus. La première étape est de montrer que l'IA peut d'abord aider avec, et ensuite conduire, les découvertes biologiques. La découverte de Claude est la dernière d'une série de travaux antérieurs similaires qui remontent à des décennies, commençant par des systèmes comme CRISPR, et se poursuivant avec des découvertes comme la recombinase pont et VIPR ces dernières années. Récemment, l'intérêt s'est accru pour les systèmes basés sur les enzymes transcriptase inverse (RT), l'enzyme sous-jacente au système identifié par Claude. Et plus récemment, une équipe de Stanford travaillant indépendamment a décrit un nouveau système RT avec un ensemble non codant associé qui est en quelque sorte similaire à celui trouvé par Claude, bien qu'il s'agisse de systèmes distincts qui ont évolué indépendamment l'un de l'autre. Je crois que nous ne faisons que commencer à trouver de tels systèmes et à les développer en outils puissants pour la biotechnologie. Je suis fier des ressources qu'Anthropic a investies pour accélérer les bénéfices publics de l'IA à travers les sciences de la vie, et nous visons à la fois à développer notre équipe des sciences de la vie et à travailler avec d'autres scientifiques pour étendre cette approche à un large éventail de problèmes. Nous ne comprenons pas encore ce que fait ce système, mais seule une poignée de systèmes connus partagent ses caractéristiques, et tous sont capables de couper, copier et coller de l'ADN. Historiquement, la découverte de tels systèmes programmables a contribué à révolutionner la médecine. CRISPR, par exemple, est maintenant le fondement des médicaments génétiques. Mais il faudra beaucoup plus de travail pour apprendre ce que fait ce système, et si on peut l'utiliser de manière similaire. actu.text_original: Today we announced the Claude-led discovery of a molecular machine that we suspect could represent a new gene editing mechanism. Its precise function, biotechnological utility (if any), or level of significance is not yet clear, but at minimum it is work I would have been proud to do as a PhD student. The work was done mostly, though not entirely, by Claude: our life sciences team suggested a broad area of research, Claude read through the literature and a bunch of genome data and discovered something interesting, then Claude proposed experiments to verify the discovery and our team carried them out. It’s easy to dismiss this as a one-off or curiosity, but we’ve repeatedly seen a pattern where AI performance in new intellectual domains goes from weak to superhuman in a matter of a few years. In 2023 models struggled to do math at the level of an average high-school student. In 2024 they started to do well on math competitions for the best high-schoolers in the country, in 2025 they started to solve minor open problems, in early 2026 more significant open problems, and in late 2026 they are beginning to solve the top few open problems in all of mathematics. We believe AI for biology is on a similar exponential trend. The main difference between biology and mathematics, of course, is that math can be done purely theoretically, while biology requires experimentation. Some have used this to draw the conclusion that AI’s utility in biology will be limited. We think this is wrong. As we’ve demonstrated today, humans can collaborate with AI to perform the experiments, validate key results in a few weeks and, if necessary, work with the AI to iterate on what they find. Eventually it may even be possible for Claude itself to safely perform the experiments by autonomously controlling lab equipment, with appropriate safeguards in place, but we aren’t doing that today (our lab is also a BSL1/BSL2 facility that doesn't handle materials dangerous to humans). More broadly, biomedical advancement has many stages — from fundamental biology discoveries, to translational research, to drug discovery, clinical trials, and finally the actual delivery of medicines and health care to patients. We are also interested in these later stages, but even simply accelerating the first stage of fundamental biological discoveries has the potential to speed up and broaden the entire pipeline. Improving our understanding of biology and sharpening biologists’ tools can drive forward all of the later stages, for example by identifying new drug targets, finding new therapeutic modalities, allowing for more precise measurement, and speeding up the experimental loop which itself further accelerates our understanding of biology. This will not in itself speed up clinical trial times, but if it succeeds it could greatly increase the number of promising candidates that go into the pipeline — an increase in throughput even though latency remains. In Machines of Loving Grace, I wrote about AI’s potential to “cure most diseases in 5-10 years” — a goal that sounds impossible, but one I believe is just barely possible if AI is applied to every stage of the pipeline. The first step is showing that AI can first help with, and then drive, biological discoveries. Claude’s discovery is the latest in a line of related prior work that goes back decades, beginning with systems like CRISPR, and continuing with discoveries like the bridge recombinase and VIPR in the past few years. Recently, there has been heightened interest in systems based on reverse transcriptase (RT) enzymes, the enzyme underlying the system Claude identified. And most recently, a Stanford team working independently described a novel RT system with an associated non-coding array that is in some ways similar to the one Claude found, though they are distinct systems that evolved independently from each other. I believe that we’re at the very beginning of finding such systems and developing them into powerful tools for biotechnology. I’m proud of the resources Anthropic has invested in accelerating the public benefits of AI through the life sciences, and we’re aiming both to grow our life sciences team and to work with other scientists to extend this approach to a broad range of problems. If you have a proposal for a research collaboration or are interested in joining our life sciences team, please reach out. Beside the enzyme’s gene sits a long array of repeating DNA—a structure that looks somewhat similar to CRISPR. We don’t yet understand what this system does, but only a handful of known systems share its features, and all of them are able to cut, copy, and paste DNA. Historically, the discovery of such programmable systems has helped revolutionize medicine. CRISPR, for instance, is now the foundation of genetic medicines. But it will take much more work to learn what this system does, and whether it can be put to similar use. actu.text_fr: La semaine dernière, l'ouragan Isaias a touché terre dans le Panhandle de Floride. Nos pensées vont à toutes les personnes affectées et aux efforts de rétablissement en cours. Basé sur les évaluations initiales, voici comment notre modèle a soutenu la réponse à #Isaias : - Suivi de la trajectoire de l'ouragan : WeatherNext a été le modèle le plus précis sur la trajectoire de la tempête. Alors que les modèles physiques traditionnels prévoyaient un atterrissage plus proche de la Nouvelle-Orléans, WeatherNext a correctement prédit une trajectoire plus à l'est. Cela a permis aux prévisionnistes du NHC de souligner le potentiel d'impacts éoliens et de ondes de tempête dans le Panhandle de Floride dès leur toute première prévision. - Plus de temps pour se préparer : Jusqu'à trois jours avant l'atterrissage, notre modèle a constamment prédit son emplacement éventuel dans le Panhandle de Floride à moins de 60 km, aidant le NHC à affiner sa trajectoire vers le Panhandle de Floride et à émettre des alertes et des avertissements d'ouragan pour donner aux responsables en Floride, en Alabama et au Mississippi plus de temps pour se préparer. - Indications précoces sur l'intensité : Au début, WeatherNext a prédit avec précision l'intensification en un ouragan majeur. Aux côtés des modèles régionaux d'ouragans HWRF et HMON, les prévisions d'intensité de WeatherNext ont aidé les prévisionnistes du NHC à prédire qu'Isaias approcherait la côte en tant qu'ouragan de catégorie 2 dès le premier bulletin. Donner aux communautés plus de temps et des avertissements plus précis est essentiel pour protéger les vies et les moyens de subsistance. Bien que les performances du modèle varient d'une tempête à l'autre, Isaias reflète nos découvertes plus larges. Dans notre récent article @Nature co-écrit avec les prévisionnistes du NHC, évaluant plus de 200 cyclones tropicaux mondiaux, nous avons constaté que notre modèle fournit environ 1 jour de préavis supplémentaire pour la trajectoire et l'intensité. Ce fut un honneur pour les équipes @GoogleDeepMind et @GoogleResearch de travailler aux côtés des prévisionnistes du NHC. En combinant l'IA, les modèles physiques, les données satellitaires et l'expertise cruciale des météorologues, nous sommes enthousiastes à l'idée de continuer à repousser les limites des prévisions pour aider à protéger les communautés.
actu.text_original: Last week, Hurricane Isaias made landfall in the Florida Panhandle. Our thoughts are with everyone affected and with the recovery efforts still underway. Based on initial evaluations, here's how our model supported the response to #Isaias : - Tracking the Hurricane’s Path: WeatherNext was the most accurate model on the storm’s track. While traditional physics models predicted landfall closer to New Orleans, WeatherNext correctly predicted a path further east. This allowed NHC forecasters to highlight the potential for wind and storm surge impacts in the Florida Panhandle from their very first forecast. - More Time to Prepare: Up to three days before landfall, our model consistently predicted its eventual location in the Florida Panhandle to within 60 km or less, supporting the NHC as they honed in on a track toward the Florida Panhandle and issued hurricane watches and warnings to give officials in Florida, Alabama, and Mississippi more time to prepare. - Early Indications about Intensity: Early on, WeatherNext accurately predicted the intensification to a major hurricane. Alongside the regional hurricane models HWRF and HMON, WeatherNext’s intensity forecasts helped NHC forecasters to predict that the Isaias would approach the coast as a category 2 hurricane from the very first advisory. Giving communities more time and more accurate warnings is critical for protecting lives and livelihoods. While model performance varies from storm to storm, Isaias reflects our broader findings. In our recent @Nature paper co-authored with NHC forecasters, evaluating 200+ global tropical cyclones, we found our model provides ~1 day of additional lead time for both track and intensity. It’s been an honor for the @GoogleDeepMind and @GoogleResearch teams to work alongside NHC forecasters. By combining AI, physics models, satellite data, and the crucial expertise of meteorologists, we're excited to keep pushing the boundaries of forecasting to help protect communities.

Souligne l'opportunité pour les défenseurs d'utiliser ces outils pour sécuriser leurs logiciels à des niveaux sans précédent : Oege de Moor (@oegerikus) Pour la deuxième fois dans l'histoire de Google Chrome, Google a attribué une prime de 250 000 $ pour un exploit complet… à @XBOW. Voici l'histoire complète : Lors d'une réunion générale début 2026 à Malte, j'ai lancé à l'équipe un défi fou. Un exploit complet de Chrome d'ici la conférence annuelle de cybersécurité Black Hat en août. Je pensais qu'il y avait peu de meilleurs tests pour savoir si @XBOW pouvait passer des applications web aux logiciels de bureau, aux serveurs et aux appareils. Chrome est l'un des logiciels les plus robustes de la planète, utilisé par plus de la moitié de la population mondiale. Un exploit complet permet à un attaquant de prendre le contrôle total d'une machine, où il peut lire chaque e-mail, mot de passe et identifiant bancaire que l'utilisateur tape. Vous n'avez pas besoin de télécharger quoi que ce soit ni de cliquer sur un lien de phishing. Visiter le faux site suffit. Alors @moyix, Andres Luksenberg, Baul Lee et Willem Pinckaers ont relevé le défi avec un cinquième coéquipier : GPT-5.6 Sol d'OpenAI. Ils ont construit une chaîne qu'ils pensaient gagnante, mais Google nous a dit qu'ils connaissaient déjà l'un des bugs. Nous étions déjà à Las Vegas pour Black Hat et DEF CON, et l'équipe ne voulait pas rentrer sans la victoire. Alors Brendan et les agents ont construit un nouvel exploit en seulement 6 jours. Nous l'avons soumis à Google et avons attendu. La nouvelle est tombée que nous avions fait ce qui aurait dû être impossible. Une prime pour une chaîne d'exploitation complète de 250 000 $, la première attribuée selon les règles 2026 de Google. Il a fallu seulement 6 jours et 40 000 $ de calcul pour construire un exploit qui affecte un milliard d'utilisateurs de Chrome sous Windows. Un vétéran des services de renseignement m'a dit que son équipe passait 6 mois sur ce type de vulnérabilité. Ma conclusion : le coût de la découverte de vulnérabilités vraiment critiques s'effondre, tant pour les attaquants que pour les défenseurs. Restreindre les modèles puissants n'est pas la solution ; GPT-5.6 Sol est déjà public. Mais les défenseurs ont un avantage que les attaquants n'auront jamais : ils peuvent tester leur propre code en premier. Supposez que votre logiciel est exploitable. Quiconque chasse vos bugs a les mêmes éléments constitutifs que nous. C'est une cause d'urgence mais pas de panique. XBOW développe maintenant un produit autonome pour tester les logiciels compilés (applications de bureau, serveurs, appareils embarqués) et s'associe aux plus grandes organisations mondiales pour concevoir ce produit. Si vous souhaitez en faire partie, contactez-nous. P.S. Redémarrez Chrome chaque fois que le bouton Mettre à jour apparaît !

idees.text_fr: 2/2 Deuxièmement, sur la communication autour de l'IA. Je ne suis pas d'accord pour dire que ma communication a été disproportionnément négative. En fait, elle a été à peu près également équilibrée entre les risques et les avantages : j'ai écrit un essai majeur sur chacun, et même dans les interviews où je discute des risques, je veille à mentionner fréquemment les incroyables avantages ainsi qu'à proposer des solutions possibles aux risques (les courts extraits de mes interviews qui finissent sur les réseaux sociaux ont tendance à être disproportionnément négatifs, car cela génère des clics). En fait, j'ai écrit Machines of Loving Grace parce que je ne trouvais pas que l'industrie de l'IA peignait une image assez inspirante de la façon dont la technologie pourrait transformer radicalement le monde pour le mieux. L'essentiel de l'essai est consacré à réfuter le scepticisme quant au potentiel de l'IA dans la santé et la biologie, et à montrer pourquoi je pense qu'il sera réellement possible de guérir la plupart des maladies humaines en environ 5-10 ans, aussi fou que cela puisse paraître aux gens ordinaires et, franchement, aux biologistes aussi (j'en étais un !). Et, si vous lisez mon essai le plus récent (Policy on the AI Exponential), je discute de propositions concrètes sur la façon de rationaliser le processus de la FDA pour s'assurer que le déluge de médicaments accélérés par l'IA n'est pas ralenti par le processus réglementaire. Je ressens l'urgence ici : j'ai perdu mon père à cause de l'hépatite C quelques années seulement avant le développement des antiviraux à action directe (sofosbuvir), qui guérissent 95% des patients et l'auraient probablement guéri. Je suis d'accord que le public a une vision négative de l'IA (et que c'est un gros problème), mais je ne pense pas que ce soit principalement causé par moi ou tout autre leader de l'IA avertissant des risques de l'IA. Je pense que c'est fondamentalement une crise de confiance. Je pense que les gens ordinaires ne font pas confiance aux entreprises, aux gouvernements ou à l'industrie technologique et suspectent toujours que nous préparons une nouvelle façon de les arnaquer. Les causes de cela remontent à des décennies et l'IA n'en est que la dernière itération. Je ne pense pas qu'une campagne de marketing tape-à-l'œil avec une tournure positive (que certains ont préconisé à Anthropic de faire) soit la façon de regagner cette confiance — à ce stade, dire que l'IA va guérir le cancer est plus un cliché qu'une source d'inspiration, et la plupart des gens pensent que c'est trompeur. La chose qui fonctionnera est de *réellement guérir le cancer*. Je pense que la critique de loin la plus précise des entreprises d'IA, y compris Anthropic, est que nous n'avons pas encore tenu nos grandes promesses de bénéficier au monde. Cela nous est totalement imputable, et je pense que c'est la critique que vous devriez faire, au lieu de toutes ces histoires de communication et de marketing. Nous faisons cependant de notre mieux pour y remédier : Anthropic intensifie très rapidement ses efforts en biologie et en médecine, et nous espérons avoir des résultats incroyables dans les années à venir et quelques lueurs précoces dans les mois à venir. Lorsque nous aurons réellement accompli quelque chose de concret, le monde entier en entendra parler, aussi fort que possible, vous avez ma parole. Mais d'ici là, je ne veux pas faire de promesses en l'air, et en attendant, je me sens obligé de parler honnêtement des risques très réels de l'IA et de la façon de les aborder. L'honnêteté est la bonne chose sur le fond, et en termes de crédibilité et de confiance publiques, elle n'est pas pire que, et peut en fait être meilleure que, une approche qui ignore ou distrait des risques que les gens comprennent instinctivement comme réels.
idees.text_original: 2/2 Second, on the messaging around AI. I do not agree that my messaging has been disproportionately negative. In fact it has been about equally balanced between risks and benefits: I’ve written one major essay about each, and even in interviews where I discuss the risks, I make sure to frequently mention the incredible benefits as well as proposing possible solutions to the risks (short clips from my interviews that end up on social media tend to be disproportionately negative, as that gets clicks). In fact, I wrote Machines of Loving Grace because I didn’t feel the AI industry was painting an inspiring enough picture of how the technology could radically transform the world for the better. The bulk of the essay is devoted to refuting skepticism of AI’s potential in health and biology, and showing why I think it will actually be possible to cure most human disease in ~5-10 years, as crazy as it may sound to ordinary people and frankly to biologists as well (I used to be one!). And, if you read my most recent essay (Policy on the AI Exponential), I discuss concrete proposals for how to streamline the FDA process to make sure the deluge of AI-accelerated drugs isn’t slowed down by the regulatory process. I feel the urgency here: I lost my father to Hepatitis C only a few years before the development of direct-acting antivirals (sofosbuvir), which cure 95% of patients and probably would have cured him. I do agree that the public has a negative view of AI (and that this is a big problem), but I don’t think it is primarily caused by me or any other AI leader warning about AI’s risks. I think it is fundamentally a crisis of trust. I think that ordinary people don’t trust companies, governments, or the tech industry and always suspect that we are cooking up some new way to screw them over. The causes of this go back decades and AI is just the latest iteration of it. I don’t think that a glitzy marketing campaign with a positive spin (which some have advocated that Anthropic do) is the way to win back that trust — at this point, saying that AI will cure cancer is more a cliche than it is inspiring, and most people think it is deceptive. The thing that will work is *actually curing cancer*. I think by far the most accurate criticism of AI companies including Anthropic is that we haven’t yet delivered on our big promises to benefit the world. That is totally on us, and I think it’s the criticism you should be making, instead of all this stuff about messaging and marketing. We are however doing our best to fix this: Anthropic is ramping up its efforts very quickly in biology and medicine, and we hope to have incredible results in the coming years and some early glimmers in the coming months. When we’ve actually accomplished something real, the whole world will hear about it, as loudly as possible, you have my word on that. But until then I don’t want to make empty promises, and in the meantime I feel compelled to speak honestly about the very real risks of AI and how to address them. Honesty is the right thing on the merits, and in terms of public credibility and trust it is no worse than, and may in fact be better than, an approach that ignores or distracts from risks which people instinctively understand are real.

idees.text_fr: 1/2 Merci Gavin pour cet échange particulièrement réfléchi. Je ne passe pas habituellement beaucoup de temps sur les réseaux sociaux mais je voulais m'engager ici car cela met vraiment en lumière le cœur d'une conversation importante. Premièrement, sur la réglementation, je pense que « soit la concentrer entre les mains de quelques entreprises et politiciens choisis via la réglementation, soit la distribuer largement » est un faux choix. Je sais qu'il existe une sorte de raccourci dans la Silicon Valley où réglementation = capture réglementaire = concentration du pouvoir, mais j'ai toujours trouvé que c'était une image trop simplifiée du monde. Beaucoup de gens en dehors de cette bulle considèrent la réglementation comme quelque chose qui contraint le pouvoir des entreprises et profite aux gens ordinaires. Je ne suis pas nécessairement d'accord avec cette perspective non plus, je pense plutôt que c'est compliqué et que cela dépend vraiment de ce que la « réglementation » contient. Mais en particulier, je pense que ceux qui sont dans le cadre « réglementation = capture réglementaire = concentration du pouvoir » sous-estiment souvent le pouvoir décentralisateur des processus institutionnels objectifs et équitables. Une analogie grossière est que le système judiciaire formel peut parfois sembler pompeux et élitiste, mais il fait un bien meilleur travail de défense des droits des individus vulnérables que l'alternative, la justice de la foule. À leur meilleur, les institutions peuvent investir le pouvoir dans les idées plutôt que dans les personnes, et ainsi décentraliser ce pouvoir. C'est pourquoi Anthropic a toujours fait ses propositions politiques très soigneusement. Nous nous efforçons de faire des propositions qui désavantagent (ralentissent) les entreprises d'IA de pointe tout en *avantageant* les petits concurrents. Le SB53 de Californie (que nous avons soutenu), et même le très critiqué SB 1047 (sur lequel nous étions ambivalents), exemptent complètement toute entreprise en dessous d'un certain montant de revenus ou de coûts d'entraînement de modèles (c'était 500 millions de dollars pour le SB 53, moins pour le 1047 mais nous nous y sommes opposés). Plus récemment, le processus de test que nous avons préconisé au CAISI et à la Maison Blanche implique des tests plus rigoureux pour les modèles de pointe que pour les modèles non de pointe — quelque chose qui avantage différemment les challengers. De même, la lettre « Pacing the Frontier » envisage (ou du moins l'implémentation préférée d'Anthropic l'envisage) de moduler le rythme des meilleurs modèles sans contraindre ceux qui rattrapent leur retard. Cela nuit aux intérêts commerciaux des laboratoires de pointe et aide les challengers, y compris les modèles à poids ouverts ! Dans l'ensemble, mon point de vue est que l'IA est *structurellement* une technologie qui tend à concentrer le pouvoir, pour des raisons qui n'ont rien à voir avec la réglementation (plus à voir avec les implications extrêmes des lois d'échelle). Les poids ouverts aident un peu à cela mais sont nulle part près d'une solution suffisante parce qu'ils ne font que déplacer la concentration vers ceux qui ont le plus de calcul et de puces (qui sont grosso modo les laboratoires de pointe plus peut-être les fournisseurs de matériel). Par contraste, je pense que les bonnes « règles du jeu » peuvent simultanément (a) aborder les risques cyber/bio/alignement de l'IA, (b) contraindre institutionnellement le pouvoir des entreprises d'IA de pointe, et (c) laisser de la place aux modèles à poids ouverts tout en abordant les risques spécifiques qu'ils apportent. D'ailleurs, je ne pense pas que les événements des derniers mois n'aient « pas abouti à [mon] chemin réglementaire préféré ». L'approche que l'administration Trump serait en train d'adopter — tests avant le déploiement pour les modèles de pointe, et aussi tests des modèles à poids ouverts lorsqu'ils se rapprochent de la pointe — est une approche que je soutiens beaucoup, bien sûr, je dois en voir les détails pour en être sûr. Je soutiens également les idées de Demis Hassabis concernant une entité de type FINRA.
idees.text_original: 1/2 Thanks Gavin for an especially thoughtful exchange. I don't usually spend much time on social media but I wanted to engage here because it really brings out the heart of an important conversation. First, on regulation, I think that “either concentrate it in the hands of a chosen few companies and politicians via regulation or distribute it widely” is a false choice. I know that there’s a sort of Silicon Valley shorthand where regulation = regulatory capture = concentration of power, but I’ve always found this to be an overly simplified picture of the world. Many people outside this bubble think of regulation as something that constrains corporate power and benefits ordinary people. I don’t necessarily agree with that perspective either, rather I think it’s complicated and really depends on what the “regulation” consists of. But in particular I think that those in the “regulation = regulatory capture = concentration of power” frame often underrate the decentralizing power of objective and fair institutional processes. A crude analogy is that the formal court system can sometimes feel stuffy and elitist, but it does a much better job of defending the rights of vulnerable individuals than the alternative, mob justice. At their best, institutions can vest power in ideas rather than people, and thereby decentralize that power. This is why Anthropic has always made its policy proposals very carefully. We try very hard to make proposals that disadvantage (slow down) frontier AI companies while *advantaging* smaller competitors. California’s SB53 (which we supported), and even the much-maligned SB 1047 (which we were ambivalent on), completely exempt any company below a certain amount of revenue or model training costs from being covered at all (it was $500M for SB 53, lower for 1047 but we objected to that). More recently the testing process we’ve advocated for at CAISI and the White House involves more rigorous tests for frontier models than off-frontier models — something that differentially advantages challengers. Similarly, the “Pacing the Frontier” letter envisions (or at least Anthropic’s preferred implementation of it envisions) modulating the pace of the very best models while not constraining those who are catching up. This hurts the business interests of the frontier labs and helps challengers, including open-weights! Overall my view is that AI is *structurally* a technology that tends to concentrate power, for reasons that have nothing to do with regulation (more to do with the extreme implications of the scaling laws). Open-weights do help some with this but are nowhere near a sufficient solution because they simply shift the concentration somewhat to those with the most compute and chips (which are roughly the frontier labs plus maybe hardware providers). By contrast I think the right “rules of the road” can simultaneously (a) address AI’s cyber/bio/alignment risks, (b) institutionally constrain the power of the frontier AI companies, and (c) leave room for open-weights models while also addressing the specific risks that they bring. BTW I do not think that the events of the last few months have “failed to result in [my] preferred regulatory path”. The approach that the Trump administration is reported to be taking — pre-deployment testing for frontier models, and also testing of open-weights models when they get closer to the frontier — is one that I am very supportive of, though of course I have to see the details to be sure. I am also supportive of Demis Hassabis’ ideas around a FINRA-like entity. This contrasts with six months ago when most of the industry was still pushing for preemption of all state regulation and no apparent federal approach either. Gavin Baker (@GavinSBaker) Sholto, thank you for setting the record straight. Larger issue is that multiple very serious people in Silicon Valley have heard some variation of this and believe it to be true. And the reason it is believable to so many is that it is consistent with Dario’s public messaging and what he outlined in the essay you shared: this technology *might* be dangerous for humans in multiple ways, could lead to extreme concentration of economic power (as outlined in the essay) and therefore needs to be regulated thoughtfully. I agree with the potential risks and I believe Dario makes all of these arguments in good faith. As discussed on the pod, if one agrees that AI *might* be dangerous, there are two ways to address this potential risk. Either concentrate it in the hands of a chosen few companies and politicians via regulation or distribute it widely. Essentially boils down to whether one believes AI is too dangerous to concentrate or too dangerous to distribute. There are reasonable arguments on both sides, but I profoundly agree with Zuckerberg’s statement that: “The notion that AI is so dangerous that the only safe path is an extreme concentration of power seems inherently problematic. Historically, hoping that an absolute power will benevolently provide for humanity if sufficiently enlightened has not led to safe or positive outcomes.” And as Dario says in the aforementioned essay, “some may object that we can simply keep AIs in check with a balance of power between many AI systems, as we do with humans.” I believe this is the best path forward: I want as many AIs as possible to maximize the odds that one shares my own particular values. And as Dario notes, no human has ever been able to take over the world. At this point, I think safe to say that Dario has lost the argument. His messaging has failed to result in his preferred regulatory path. The fact that the only solution to the recent incident where an unreleased advanced OpenAI model hacked Hugging Face was an open-source model likely ended any chance of strict near-term regulation. Essentially every major company other than Anthropic has signed Jensen’s letter. However, Dario’s messaging has been massively helpful to efforts to ban datacenters here in America. I suspect we will see anti-datacenter advocacy groups runnings ads using clips of Dario warning about how dangerous AI could be for humans. His good faith efforts in favor of regulation are now increasing the odds that AI will not be beneficial for Americans and humans everywhere. I believe that there is a reasonable chance AI might help us cure most forms of disease such that we have extended lifespans and can enjoy these long lives in an abundant Star Trek like future. That is the future that I want and I think Dario is decreasing the odds of that future at this point. He is about to be the CEO of one of the most important public companies in the world and given that the pro-regulatory effort has failed (at least for now), I respectfully think he should make an effort to be a more positive advocate for his own industry. And if I am wrong and we do need to regulate this technology, he will be a more effective advocate for this in the future having been open-minded to the alternative. And for the sake of clarity and as I outlined on the pod, I think Anthropic has deep competitive advantages and is an amazing company. Ironically, the main risk I saw to Anthropic a few months ago was nationalization as a result of Dario’s own rhetoric and behavior. — https://nitter.kareem.one/GavinSBaker/status/2088611616577253502#m
